Conditional LATE from supplied nuisance predictions

Source: vignettes/conditional-late.Rmd
conditional-late.Rmd

clate_dnn() estimates a conditional local average treatment effect from externally supplied nuisance predictions. This supported workflow uses a binary instrument A and binary treatment D. For example, an encouragement may change participation without determining it perfectly. Under the IV assumptions, the target is the effect among people whose treatment changes with encouragement, conditional on a reporting profile.

The full adjustment vector V=(X,Z)V=(X,Z) contains the pre-instrument covariates needed for instrument exogeneity. Reporting uses only XX. The effect therefore averages over the distribution of the additional controls ZZ at each reporting profile, with compliance weights. It generally differs from population CATE.

Causal interpretation requires consistency, exclusion, conditional instrument independence given VV, monotonicity, instrument overlap and positive local compliance. Without those causal assumptions, the calculation estimates a standardized observed-data Wald functional wherever its denominator is nonzero. Predictions alone do not verify identification.

An example with known nuisance functions

clate_demo_data() generates a bounded model with endogenous treatment, a conditionally valid instrument and known nuisance functions. The latent compliance rank also affects untreated outcomes. Its default data frame contains observed variables and explicitly labelled oracle prediction columns; latent variables are available only with keep_latent = TRUE.

demo <- clate_demo_data(n = 120, seed = 20261017, heterogeneous = TRUE)
d <- demo$data
X <- as.matrix(d[c("X1", "X2")])
targets <- rbind(c(.25, .25), c(.5, .5), c(.75, .75))
data.frame(targets,
           CLATE = demo$truth$theta(targets), CATE = demo$truth$cate(targets))
#>     X1   X2      CLATE   CATE
#> 1 0.25 0.25 0.06542969 0.0625
#> 2 0.50 0.50 0.12792969 0.1250
#> 3 0.75 0.75 0.19042969 0.1875

With heterogeneous = TRUE, CLATE exceeds CATE by 3/10243/1024. The default model instead has the same treatment effect for everyone at a given XX, so the targets coincide. Neither model turns a single draw’s confidence interval into evidence of repeated-sampling coverage.

The five prediction vectors have the following roles:

Argument Function evaluated at each observed ViV_i
e P(A=1∣V)P(A=1\mid V), instrument propensity
m_y0, m_y1 E[Y∣A=0,V]E[Y\mid A=0,V], E[Y∣A=1,V]E[Y\mid A=1,V]
m_d0, m_d1 E[D∣A=0,V]E[D\mid A=0,V], E[D∣A=1,V]E[D\mid A=1,V]

Arm indices refer to the instrument. The outcome regressions do not condition on participation as an extra control. In an application, supply aligned predictions from the chosen learning procedure. One full-sample nuisance state can contain five fitted regressions. The training label records their provenance; it does not train or validate them.

Matrix inputs and the two augmented signals 

fit <- clate_dnn(
  X = X, X0 = targets, Y = d$Y, D = d$D, A = d$A,
  e = d$e_oracle, m_y0 = d$m_y0_oracle, m_y1 = d$m_y1_oracle,
  m_d0 = d$m_d0_oracle, m_d1 = d$m_d1_oracle,
  s = 16L, training = "oracle", row_ids = d$row_id,
  return = c("W", "dx", "nuisance")
)

The wrapper constructs the augmented contrast for each response R=Y,DR=Y,D:

ϕR=mR,1−mR,0+Ae(R−mR,1)−1−A1−e(R−mR,0). \phi_R=m_{R,1}-m_{R,0} +\frac A e(R-m_{R,1}) -\frac{1-A}{1-e}(R-m_{R,0}).

It then solves the affine equation ∑iwi(x)(θϕD,i−ϕY,i)=0\sum_iw_i(x)(\theta\phi_{D,i}-\phi_{Y,i})=0. The result is a ratio of weighted averages, with common weights for both signals. Do not average observation-level signal ratios.

The constructor and generic ratio engine are also available separately:

signals <- iv_augmented_signals(
  Y = d$Y, D = d$D, A = d$A, e = d$e_oracle,
  m_y0 = d$m_y0_oracle, m_y1 = d$m_y1_oracle,
  m_d0 = d$m_d0_oracle, m_d1 = d$m_d1_oracle,
  row_ids = d$row_id, training = "oracle"
)
ratio <- affine_ratio_dnn(
  X = X, X0 = targets, numerator = signals$phi_y, denominator = signals$phi_d,
  s = 16L, row_ids = signals$row_ids
)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(ratio$theta, fit$theta)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(ratio$theta_vcov, fit$theta_vcov)))

Both high-level estimators use the same weighting controls as cate_dnn() and np_dnn(): method = "exact" or "asymp", 1 <= k <= s, and normalize for asymptotic weights. Exact DNN and k = 1L are the defaults. Supply a deterministic integer s, or an existing tuning specification. Without either, the package’s paper-default rule resolves the order. Covariance requires s < n. The same order and weight rule are used after every deletion and retained by predict() and diagnostics(). CATE and CLATE expose single-scale DNN only; the two-scale np_tdnn() regression method has no corresponding justification here.

For example, the generic composition can use asymptotic DNN while retaining the default single neighbor per subsample:

approximate <- affine_ratio_dnn(
  X = X, X0 = targets, numerator = signals$phi_y, denominator = signals$phi_d,
  s = 16L, method = "asymp", k = 1L, normalize = TRUE
)
summary(approximate)$coefficients
#>             estimate std.error  statistic   p.value    conf.low conf.high
#> target_1 -0.10497893 0.1940726 -0.5409261 0.5885585 -0.48535418 0.2753963
#> target_2  0.20472288 0.1326690  1.5431097 0.1228042 -0.05530365 0.4647494
#> target_3  0.03246375 0.1059318  0.3064590 0.7592552 -0.17515872 0.2400862

Availability of a weighting option is a computational contract. Statistical validity still requires the localization, bias and nuisance conditions for that choice; it does not extend an exact, single-neighbor theorem automatically.

Data frames and tibbles

Select all columns explicitly. Tibbles follow the same data-frame path; there is no formula interface or implicit column guessing.

estimate_from_table <- function(data) {
  clate_dnn(
    data = data, x_cols = c("X1", "X2"), X0 = targets,
    y_col = "Y", d_col = "D", a_col = "A", e_col = "e_oracle",
    m_y0_col = "m_y0_oracle", m_y1_col = "m_y1_oracle",
    m_d0_col = "m_d0_oracle", m_d1_col = "m_d1_oracle",
    s = 16L, training = "oracle", row_ids = data$row_id
  )
}
table_fit <- estimate_from_table(d)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(table_fit$theta, fit$theta)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(table_fit$component_vcov, fit$component_vcov)))
if (requireNamespace("tibble", quietly = TRUE)) {
  tibble_fit <- estimate_from_table(tibble::as_tibble(d))
  stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(tibble_fit$theta, fit$theta)))
}

Every observation and prediction vector must be finite and aligned in the same row order. Row IDs must be unique, finite/nonmissing numeric or nonempty character values. IDs document alignment; the wrapper cannot detect a separately permuted prediction vector supplied without its own row map. Align external predictions before passing them.

Instrument propensities must lie in [0,1] and are clipped to [clip,1-clip]; the default is clip = 1e-8. Raw and used propensities are retained by the constructor. Treatment predictions must lie in [0,1]; outcome predictions are finite but not automatically capped. Clipping a propensity does not establish overlap, and clipping predictions does not bound an unbounded observed outcome.

For CLATE, the numerator is the adjusted outcome reduced form and the denominator is the adjusted treatment first stage. component_vcov retains their full paired covariance. vcov(fit) returns ratio variance matrices on the estimator scale; theta_omega multiplies those matrices by neff. Do not divide the returned ratio variance by neff again.

info <- as.data.frame(diagnostics(fit))
fields <- c("target_id", "denominator_se", "denominator_stat",
            "instrument_1_mass", "radius_90", "jk_top1_sq_share")
knitr::kable(info[fields], digits = 4, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Target", "First-stage SE", "First-stage stat.",
                           "Instrument mass", "Radius (90%)", "Largest share"))
Target First-stage SE First-stage stat. Instrument mass Radius (90%) Largest share
target_1 0.2493 1.5644 0.6264 0.1954 0.2407
target_2 0.2831 1.7662 0.4567 0.1807 0.5059
target_3 0.2056 3.2981 0.3137 0.2115 0.3825

These diagnostics describe first-stage variation, instrument support, physical localization and concentration of fitted uncertainty. neff measures reporting-weight concentration, not the number of compliers. There is no automatic weak-instrument cutoff or target filtering.

The same plotting workflow as CATE

The fitted object determines the implementation behind each shared call. plot_estimates(), plot() and ggplot2::autoplot() use the same profile, forest and pointrange styles as CATE. The coefficient extractor plot_data_estimates() returns the common tidy table, while summary(fit)$coefficients uses the same six columns as CATE. Undefined ratios and unavailable Wald bounds remain visible in the tables.

if (requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)) {
  print(plot_estimates(fit, style = "forest"))
  print(plot_overlap(fit, type = "mass"))
  print(plot_influence(fit, targets = 2L))
}

#> Ignoring unknown labels:
#> • colour : "target"

The remaining common calls are plot_weights(fit, type = "profile"), type = "cumulative" or "kernel", plot_overlap(fit, type = "propensity"), and plot_dashboard(fit). Weight and overlap panels require W; the physical-distance weight view also requires dx, so retain both as above. Plots require optional ggplot2. Dashboards use patchwork when installed and otherwise return a named list of plots. Unavailable panels are omitted or replaced by diagnostics using the same policy as CATE.

CLATE overlap panels use instrument arms and the instrument propensity, not treatment uptake. Its influence panel shows the weighted paired score residual w * (phi_y - theta * phi_d). These are neither individual causal effects nor jackknife pseudo-values. The latter are separately available through return = "pseudo_values".

Tuning sensitivity and candidate views

As for CATE and NP regression, tuning_mode = "grid" retains the default fit and adds common candidate, estimate and diagnostic tables. All candidates reuse the same signals and frozen ranks. This is a sensitivity analysis; it does not select an order or justify inference after data-dependent selection.

grid_fit <- clate_dnn(
  X = X, X0 = targets, Y = d$Y, D = d$D, A = d$A,
  e = d$e_oracle, m_y0 = d$m_y0_oracle, m_y1 = d$m_y1_oracle,
  m_d0 = d$m_d0_oracle, m_d1 = d$m_d1_oracle,
  tuning_mode = "grid", method = "asymp", training = "oracle",
  return = c("W", "dx")
)
head(grid_fit$tuning_grid$candidates)
#>   candidate_id computed_key is_default feasible reason status lambda  s
#> 1   lambda_0p3         s_10      FALSE     TRUE     ok     ok   0.30 10
#> 2   lambda_0p4         s_14       TRUE     TRUE     ok     ok   0.40 14
#> 3   lambda_0p5         s_18      FALSE     TRUE     ok     ok   0.50 18
#> 4  lambda_0p75         s_27      FALSE     TRUE     ok     ok   0.75 27
views <- candidate_fits(grid_fit)
selected <- candidate_fit(grid_fit, 1L)
summary(selected)$coefficients
#>             estimate  std.error  statistic   p.value    conf.low conf.high
#> target_1 -0.07195888 0.18138100 -0.3967278 0.6915682 -0.42745912 0.2835413
#> target_2  0.17090655 0.10459837  1.6339313 0.1022733 -0.03410249 0.3759156
#> target_3  0.09387875 0.08431531  1.1134247 0.2655261 -0.07137622 0.2591337

Candidate views have the same class and reporting methods as a scalar fit, with paired components and covariance recomputed from cached state. They retain instrument information for overlap plots and use the candidate order for prediction. Selecting an infeasible candidate gives an actionable error. candidate_fits(fit, ids) can restrict the list to feasible candidate IDs.

if (requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)) {
  print(plot_estimates(grid_fit, candidates = "all", style = "pointrange"))
  print(plot_tuning(grid_fit))
}

plot_data_estimates(grid_fit, candidates = "all"), candidate-aware plot_weights() and diagnostics() use the same selection grammar as CATE. plot_tuning() also works from a scalar fit’s retained state. Stored grid fits reuse their stored standard errors; refit with se = TRUE if these were omitted and confidence bounds are needed.

A selected one-sided model

When the design implies D(0)=0D(0)=0, select one_sided = TRUE and omit m_d0, or provide an identically zero vector. The wrapper checks D <= A. That observed check alone does not establish the counterfactual restriction.

For a simple example, specify perfect compliance, D(a)=aD(a)=a, and a constant effect. Here the first-stage signal is identically one and the estimate and covariance reduce to CATE.

set.seed(320)
n <- 32L
one_X <- matrix(seq(-1, 1, length.out = n), ncol = 1)
A <- rbinom(n, 1, .5)
baseline <- .2 * one_X[, 1]
Y <- baseline + .5 * A + rnorm(n, sd = .1)
one <- clate_dnn(
  X = one_X, x0 = 0, Y = Y, D = A, A = A, e = rep(.5, n),
  m_y0 = baseline, m_y1 = baseline + .5, m_d1 = rep(1, n),
  one_sided = TRUE, s = 6L, training = "oracle", return = "signals"
)
one$components
#>      numerator denominator
#> [1,] 0.5191015           1
stopifnot(all(one$signals[, 2] == 1))

In general one-sided models, an eligible nonparticipant’s augmented first-stage signal can be negative. The implementation preserves it.

New reporting profiles

predict() changes only the reporting profiles. It reuses the original observations, frozen signals, metric and resolved order; it fits no nuisance functions and does not predict outcomes for new households.

predict(fit, X0 = rbind(c(.4, .4), c(.6, .6)), se.fit = TRUE)
#> $fit
#> [1] 0.1883769 0.1920315
#> 
#> $se.fit
#> [1] 0.1348139 0.1088746
predict(table_fit, newdata = data.frame(X1 = .5, X2 = .5), interval = "confidence")
#>            fit         lwr       upr
#> [1,] 0.2079148 -0.06418391 0.4800136

Undefined ratios remain visible

An exactly zero aggregate denominator gives an undefined ratio, while preserving the components and their covariance. This is different from a finite negative denominator, which remains a computed signed ratio.

zero <- affine_ratio_dnn(
  X = matrix(1:4), x0 = 0, numerator = c(2, 1, 4, 3),
  denominator = rep(0, 4), s = 2
)
zero$components
#>      numerator denominator
#> [1,]         2           0
zero$status
#>             target_id     ratio_status negative_denominator
#> denominator         1 zero_denominator                FALSE
#>             near_zero_denominator covariance_status wald_available
#> denominator                 FALSE                ok          FALSE
confint(zero)
#>          conf.low conf.high
#> target_1       NA        NA
ratio_confidence_set(zero$components, zero$component_vcov)
#> Paired ratio confidence sets
#>   target 1: unresolved  (coefficient_rounding)

For the covariance derivation, exact worked arrays, confidence-set geometry and pointwise inference conditions, continue with Paired frozen-score inference. Full-sample inference needs learner accuracy and deletion stability as well as orthogonality and undersmoothing. The software’s numerical statuses do not certify those conditions or causal validity. The existing local IV-GMM workflow uses a different moment and covariance route; it is not an alias for this augmented CLATE estimator.
